source.title: Training transformers for mesh-based simulations
source.authors: Paul Garnier; V. Lannelongue; J. Viquerat; E. Hachem

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper runs its own scaling sweeps on graph-based physics models and reports an exponent different from cited language-model studies. It also argues that the scaling curve may bend; this is a refinement of the scaling-law claim in a different domain.
record.gate_note: The scaling results concern graph transformers for physics simulation, not language-model held-out cross-entropy. The paper also reports correlations between training loss, FLOPs, and rollout RMSE; those are recorded as related findings, not as downstream-task results. Cited language-model scaling results are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The authors run their own isoFLOP sweeps (over 60 graph transformers, 50k–50M parameters) on mesh-based physics simulation. They fit a power law for compute-optimal parameter count versus FLOPs, giving a scaling result in a non-text setting. That makes it T3, a new setting with a result on the claim, rather than T5. Their curvature argument rests on comparing with exponents cited from Kaplan and Hoffmann, not on their own refutation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find N∝C^0.75 on 3D-Coarse Aneurysm, much higher than Hoffmann's 0.50 and close to Kaplan's 0.73. They conclude that transformers follow similar power laws across very different domains. They read the comparison with the larger-model language-model studies as evidence of curvature, with the exponent decreasing for larger models. Cylinder gives a very similar, slightly larger exponent.
record.recipe_differences: This is a graph-physics scaling sweep using optimal parameter count versus training FLOPs and rollout-related objectives, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling. Training runs use matched cosine schedules; the paper does not test the original language-model recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported fit differs across datasets: the cylinder sweep uses 1500 rather than 10000 tokens per iteration and a smaller model and FLOPs range, and is described as having a slightly larger exponent. The main sweep uses six FLOPs budgets and matched cosine schedules.

fits_no_version.finding: Training loss and test All-Rollout RMSE are strongly correlated across models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In graph-physics models, training loss predicts rollout evaluation error.

record.problems: The scaling analysis is on graph-based physics models rather than language models. The paper does not report uncertainty for the fitted exponents, gives no exact cylinder exponent in the text, and describes the main sweep's selected objective inconsistently as validation All-Rollout RMSE and final training loss. Its argument about curvature partly compares its result with results cited from other papers.

untested.parts: No extrapolation from small to much larger runs is checked numerically. The 50M XL model is trained as the predicted optimum, but its loss is not compared to a prediction.
No language-model allocation. No token-versus-compute exponent is reported even in the graph setting.
Depth and width at fixed parameter count are not compared. The Figure 4 ablations vary size, not shape at fixed size.
Image, video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. The power-law form of loss versus compute is not explicitly fitted.
Parameter counting, schedule and fitting method are not varied. Curvature is inferred only from comparison with cited papers.

missing.what: The study's XL (~50M) model, chosen as the compute-optimal size predicted by the power law, is said to 'confirm this hypothesis'. No predicted versus actual loss is reported. This is a qualitative extrapolation check relevant to V2 or V5.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's main contribution is a graph-physics architecture; scaling is one section. All exponent comparisons with language models use cited values. The fit is on six isoFLOP minima and reports no uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute is not measured.
The paper does not test predictions of larger language-model runs from smaller runs.
The paper fits an optimal parameter-count versus FLOPs relation for graph simulation models, but does not test language-model parameter and token allocation laws.
No test of how depth, width, or other architecture details affect language-model loss at fixed parameter count.

Tests scaling in graph-based physics simulation using rollout RMSE and an optimal-parameter-count versus FLOPs fit; it does not test held-out language-model loss or the same power law across image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer settings.
No downstream language-task performance is tested.

The paper reports graph-model compute-optimal fits on two datasets and discusses curvature, but does not systematically vary parameter counting, fitting method, or other setup choices in language-model scaling experiments.

rows.subject: our transformer models
rows.operation_detail: For six FLOPs budgets, trained models with varying parameter counts and training steps; selected the local-minimum model for each budget and fit a power law.

conditions.value: cosine decay matched to the number of training steps

rows.measure: Optimal parameter count N as a function of FLOPs budget C
rows.note: The paper describes the objective as final validation All-Rollout RMSE, but also says it selects the final training loss; the text does not resolve this discrepancy. The reported exponent is for optimal model size versus compute, not held-out loss versus compute.
rows.check: This is a V5 result: a compute-optimal N∝C^0.75 fit on 3D-Coarse Aneurysm from six isoFLOP minima, in a non-text domain. It alone cannot show V7 fit-dependence. The contrast with 0.73 and 0.50 comes from cited language-model papers, so V7 is removed. No fit uncertainty is given. The selected objective is described inconsistently: validation All-Rollout RMSE in one place, final training loss in another.

rows.subject: our transformer models
rows.size_stated: smaller range of model and FLOP sizes than the 3D-C OARSE A NEURYSM sweep; exact range not stated
rows.operation_detail: Ran the same isoFLOPs search with different model sizes and training steps, then fit the local-minimum models.

conditions.value: smaller range of both FLOP and model size

rows.measure: Optimal parameter count versus FLOPs scaling fit
rows.value: Scaling described as very similar, with a slightly bigger exponent factor; exact exponent not stated.
rows.note: The paper presents this as consistent with potential curvature in the scaling laws; the cylinder exponent is not given numerically in the text.
rows.check: The Cylinder fit is described as very similar with a slightly bigger exponent; no number is given. The setup also differs (1500 vs 10000 tokens per iteration, smaller range). For V5 the same form recurs. For V7 the dataset or setup dependence is small and unquantified, so partial.

source_check.correct: V5: observed; Cylinder exhibits a similar fitted power law. V7: weak evidence of exponent variation under changed dataset, scale range and tokens per iteration; no numerical Cylinder exponent is stated.
source_check.problem: The partial state does not fit V5: the paper reports similar power-law scaling, with no stated weakening or failure of that form.
